tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

7. Failures call `snapshot()` and wait for a human to resolve them.
8. After the steps, `expect.js` runs through `executor.check`. `expect.text` waits for a human verdict.
9. Every state change calls `executor.render(state)`, which paints the panel and HUD.

```ts
export type Step = { id: string; why: string; do?: Action; use?: string; with?: Record<string, unknown>; source?: StepSource; approved?: boolean; };
  ```

### D. How to run it in Obsidian

**(i) In-app.** Inject core plus the overlay into the renderer and write an Obsidian in-page Executor:
- `run`: port the executor but replace the palette with `app.commands.executeCommandById` or the `.prompt` palette.
- `open`: `proof.obsidian.open`.
- `check`: indirect eval.
- `snapshot`: `.modal`, `.notice`, `.prompt` and active-leaf text.
- `render`: bar and stage.

Problems:
- Synthetic input is untrusted. CM6 relies on `beforeinput`/DOM mutation and native selection, so `typeText` into the editor is unreliable.
- tldraw needs real pointer events (my memory note `reference_tldraw_store_put_no_listener`).
- Escape is caught by the modal keymap scope. Whether a synthetic keydown reaches Obsidian's keymap is unverified.
- The Settings window is a separate renderer in 1.13, so an in-page runner can't reach it.
- Outside fixtures (eng-2143-obsidian has two) can't run in the page.

**(ii) Node-side (recommended).** machine.ts runs in Node unmodified, verified by the grep above: no window, document or localStorage. The Executor wraps the harness `client`:
- `run`: inject `selector.ts` to resolve a selector into a visible, still rect, then send trusted CDP `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` and `key`/`typeText`. `open` and `command_palette` go through `client.evaluate`, and `js` goes through `client.evaluate`.
- `check`: `evaluate` of `expect.js`.
- `snapshot`: DOM text plus `client.screenshot()`. This finally makes the `screenshot` action real, which feeds pr-evidence.
- `render`: `evaluate('window.__proofHud.paint(state)')`.
- HUD: inject the bar and stage bundle once. Register `Runtime.addBinding({name:"__proofCmd"})`. HUD buttons call `__proofCmd(JSON)`, Node's `Runtime.bindingCalled` handler calls `machine.command("hud", ...)`. Re-add the binding after a plugin reload or page reload.
- Outside fixtures run in Node through `publishSql` plus psql.
- `vault`, the lock and delivery come from the existing `launch`, `deliver` and `claim` (bundle marker, bundleHash).

Why (ii): it gives trusted input for CM6 and tldraw, reaches the Settings target, can take real screenshots, and has a Node host for SQL. It also matches how Sid's own recorder attaches over CDP.

**What breaks in Obsidian, in either shape:**
- **Settings window (1.13):** a separate target. Pick the target per action and drive it by DOM; CDP mouse input doesn't reach it.
- **Escape keymap scope:** use `client.pressEscape` (trusted) or `proof.obsidian.closeModals` instead of a synthetic dispatch.
- **`.modal` overflow:** it clips popovers, and the stage ring can sit under the modal. Put the HUD at the `body` level with a high z-index.
- **tldraw canvas:** needs real pointer events, collapsed sidebars and a measured camera.
- **Contested vault plugin directory:** keep the deliver marker check and the main.js hash before and after the run.
- **Plugin reload:** `reloadPlugin` replaces the plugin but `window.proof` survives, so re-inject after `delete window.proof`.

### E. Effort for an MVP

The MVP runs one existing-style kit with 2–3 cases against a leased vault, with step/case pause modes and copy-to-PR output.

| Work | Size |
|---|---|
| Vendor core (action, kit, machine, journal, template, recipes, fixtures, helpers) and build for Node | S |
| Node CDP Executor (selector injection, trusted click/type/press, palette via commands, wait_for, when, js, check, snapshot, screenshot) | M |
| Kit loader and CLI wired into launch/deliver/claim, inject helpers, map `target.vault` to the lease | S |
| HUD over CDP: bundle bar, stage and words; `paint(state)`; `addBinding` command bridge; re-bind on reload | M |
| Pause/mode controls (already in the machine; only wiring) | S |
| Copy-to-PR: write `resultMarkdown` to a file or stdout and merge with `last-run.json` and screenshots | S |
| Outside fixtures via psql and the proof DB (optional for the MVP) | M |
| Obsidian-specific helper fixes (dialogs, Escape, Settings window) | S |

Overall about M–L (1–2 weeks). Without outside fixtures it's about M.

### F. Caveats
- **Licence and ownership:** src/index.ts:6–8 says the code under src/core and src/roam is copied from Sid's private `dg-demo-videos/proof` by its `roam/build.ts`. roam-prototypes is public but has no licence file, and the API reports `license: null`. Get Sid's agreement, and decide on a canonical home before vendoring into the discourse-graph monorepo, so two copies don't drift.
- **References into Sid's private repo:** links.ts:47–48 points at `/mnt/data/projects/dg-demo-videos/...`. The comments reference `qa.ts`, `prove.ts` and `recordDemo.ts`, which are not in the PR.
- **PR still open:** the kit format may still change.

**Not verified:**
- Whether Obsidian's keymap ignores untrusted keydown events.
- Whether CM6 accepts `execCommand("insertText")` from a synthetic focus.
- Whether `Runtime.addBinding` survives Obsidian's plugin reload.
- I didn't run vitest or any kit live. The macOS and Windows helper paths are untested by Sid's own README.

content.text:
The engine of Sid's proof kit can be used in Obsidian unchanged. What's missing is the piece that actually drives Obsidian: Sid's PR contains no runner for Obsidian kits. This comes from a full read of PR #26 at its current head (`3544177f`). Nothing was run; this is from reading the code. ## How the proof kit is built There are three layers: ``` ┌───────────────────────── core/ (no Roam, no page/browser APIs) ────────────────┐ │ kit.ts Kit → cases → steps → actions, plus setup fixtures and validation │ │ machine.ts run engine: auto / step / case modes, speeds, pause, approve, │ │ retry, verdict, leave-out │ │ recipes.ts expands a named recipe into a list of actions │ │ fixtures.ts setup steps journal.ts event log publish.ts SQL seeding │ │ helpers.ts a script (as text) that installs `window.proof` in the app page │ └────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ the one interface the engine drives Executor { run(action), check(js), snapshot(), render(state) } │ ┌──────────────────────── roam/ (the Roam-specific parts) ────────────────────────┐ │ executor.ts + input.ts run steps inside the page with simulated events │ │ bar.ts + stage.ts floating controls bar, highlight ring, on-screen cursor │ │ panel.ts, runner.ts, index.ts, page-kit.ts sidebar; kit stored as Roam blocks │ │ build-loader.ts loads the PR's CI build │ │ words.ts copy-to-PR / bug-report text (no page access) │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ helper/ a separate Node process that starts a local Supabase "proof DB" (Linux only so far) ``` **How a run goes:** 1. The kit is loaded and validated, and setup fixtures run. 2. `window.proof` helpers are added to the app page. 3. `Machine.run()` takes each case, then each step: - expands any recipe into actions - hands each action to `executor.run`, slowed to the chosen speed - pauses for a person if a step fails 4. Each case is then checked: `expect.js` runs, or for `expect.text` a person gives the verdict. 5. Every state change redraws the controls bar. 6. Results become copy-to-PR markdown. **Who can approve:** steps written by a model or by a person need an Allow before they run. Only the on-screen controls bar can approve a step or give a verdict; an agent cannot. ## What already supports Obsidian - **`proof.obsidian` helpers** in `core/helpers.ts:647–745`. These are working code, not stubs: - plugin, reloadPlugin and signIn - nodeTypes, file and frontmatter - open, write and templates - notices and closeModals The plugin id and the settings fields match our `apps/obsidian`. - **The kit format** accepts `target.app: "obsidian"` and requires a `vault` for it. - **Two real Obsidian kits:** `eng-2143-obsidian.json` (9 cases) and `eng-2176-obsidian.json` (7 cases). - **Database seeding** (`publish.ts`) already writes Obsidian-shaped rows. - **The gap:** nothing in the PR actually runs an Obsidian kit. Code comments point to Sid's private `recorder/recordDemo.ts`, which attaches over CDP and which I couldn't read. ## What can be reused for Obsidian | Verdict | Modules | |---|---| | **Use as-is** | `core/action`, `kit`, `machine`, `journal`, `template`, `recipes`, `fixtures`, `publish`; `roam/words.ts` (copy-to-PR text); `roam/selector.ts` (selector matching, runs inside the page) | | **Small adapter** | `core/helpers.ts`:
• its generic dialog helpers assume Roam's Blueprint UI
• a bug at line 9 stops the helpers being reinstalled after a plugin reload
`core/database.ts` (proof DB address is hard-coded); `bar.ts` and `stage.ts` (the controls bar has to send its commands somewhere new) | | **Rewrite** | `executor.ts` and `input.ts`. Simulated events can't type into Obsidian's editor (CodeMirror 6), can't drive tldraw, and can't press Escape past Obsidian's key handling | | **Not needed** | panel, runner, index, page-kit, roam, build-loader, agent-tools; all Roam recipes and baselines | ## Recommended setup: run the engine in Node, attached over CDP ``` Node: kit.json → Machine (unchanged) → ObsidianCdpExecutor ──CDP──► Obsidian (leased vault) ▲ built on dg-obsidian-cdp-verify's client: │ real clicks, typing and Escape; evaluate; │ screenshots; deliver.mjs to build the plugin │ machine.command("hud", …) ◄── Runtime.addBinding ◄── controls bar (bar.ts + stage.ts) added to Obsidian's page ``` **Why Node rather than running everything inside Obsidian's page:** - Real CDP input works with Obsidian's editor and with tldraw. - It can reach the separate Settings window in Obsidian 1.13. - It can take real screenshots for PR evidence. - It can run the SQL setup steps. - It reuses our existing vault lease, build delivery and bundle check. - It's most likely how Sid's own private runner works too. **Obsidian-specific problems to handle:** - **Settings window:** it's a separate CDP target in 1.13, so drive it through its DOM. - **Escape:** send it through CDP or use `closeModals`. - **Overlay placement:** `.modal` clips anything positioned inside it, so mount the controls bar on `body` with a high z-index. - **tldraw:** needs real pointer events, with the sidebars collapsed. - **Shared vault plugin folder:** keep the bundle marker and hash check, since other worktrees can overwrite the build. - **Plugin reload:** `window.proof` survives it, so delete it and reinstall the helpers. **Effort for a minimal version** (one kit, 2–3 cases, step/case pause, copy-to-PR): - About M without the SQL setup steps, M–L with them. - The two medium-sized pieces are the CDP executor and wiring the controls bar to the Node process. **Not checked:** - whether Obsidian's key handling ignores simulated key presses - whether `Runtime.addBinding` survives a plugin reload ## Ask Sid first 1. Does his private recorder already run Obsidian kits over CDP? If so, we shouldn't rebuild it. 2. Where should the proof core live? It's copied from his private repo, the repo has no licence and the PR is still open. Vendoring it into the monorepo without agreeing this means two copies drifting apart. **Suggested spike once that's answered:** run `eng-2143-obsidian.json` through the Node engine plus a CDP executor against a leased vault. I can draft the message to Sid if you like. The checkpoint and log are updated.

# Instructions for coding agents

This is a pnpm monorepo for public, installable Roam developer-extension artifacts whose source remains private.

## Creating a prototype

- Always create a workspace with `pnpm create:prototype -- --name <kebab-case> --title "<title>" --description "<public description>"`.
- Pass `--spec <file>` when a specification is provided. Read `SPEC.md` completely before implementation.
- Use `--adopt-existing` only for a placeholder containing `README.md` and optional `SPEC.md`. Preserve those documents.
- Do not copy the template by hand or create a branch/repository per prototype.

## Implementation rules

- Keep prototype code inside `prototypes/<slug>` and shared convention material inside `packages/extension-base`.
- Import `roamjs-components` directly. `packages/extension-base` is build tooling, configuration, and a template, not a browser runtime API.
- With this repository's ESM build, never default-import a published CommonJS subpath from `roamjs-components`. Import named exports from package barrels instead, such as `import { addStyle } from "roamjs-components/dom"`.
- Support both documented loading modes: Roam's developer-extension URL loader and the `roam/js` ESM loader. Treat `args.extensionAPI` as optional and provide a fallback or clearly gate features that require it; `window.roamAlphaAPI` remains available in both modes.
- Read the relevant guidance under `packages/extension-base/skills` before using Roam graph writes, commands, navigation, or React rendering.
- For new graph reads, prefer `await window.roamAlphaAPI.data.async.*`. Never use legacy top-level aliases such as `roamAlphaAPI.q`, `roamAlphaAPI.pull`, or `roamAlphaAPI.createBlock`.
- Keep `runExtension` as the lifecycle wrapper. Dispose observers, listeners, commands, timers, and mounted UI when the extension unloads.
- Never edit generated `dist` files. Build them with pnpm and the shared esbuild CLI.
- Keep all browser code and public documentation secret-free. Only `process.env.NODE_ENV` and `process.env.VERSION` are allowed.

## Validation

Run `pnpm test`, `pnpm build`, and `pnpm prepare:artifacts`. Only `extension.js`, `README.md`, optional `extension.css`, and optional `CHANGELOG.md` may be published.

content.text:
I can, but `roam-prototypes` itself is the wrong home for the Obsidian runner. Its `AGENTS.md` describes it as public "Roam developer-extension artifacts" and publishes only `extension.js`. It also says not to create a branch or repo per prototype. A Node runner that drives Obsidian over CDP doesn't fit that. Here's the plan.

## Plan

**Repo:** clone `roam-prototypes` into its own folder, `~/Desktop/code/proof-kit`, and create the branch `obsidian-runner` off `origin/proof-runner`.
- Branching keeps Sid's commit history, so the work can later go upstream to him as a PR stacked on #26, or move into a new repo, whichever you two decide.
- **Local only:** I won't push or create a GitHub repo without asking you.

**Steps:**
1. **Reuse the engine.** Import `core/*`, `roam/words.ts` and `roam/selector.ts` as they are, with no copies.
2. **Fix the helpers** in `core/helpers.ts`: allow the helpers to be reinstalled after a plugin reload (the line-9 bug), and give Obsidian its own modal and Escape handling. These are small changes on Sid's code.
3. **Add a new `obsidian/` folder:**
   - `executor.ts`: the CDP executor. Real clicks, typing and key presses; command palette through `executeCommandById`; waits, checks, and snapshots with screenshots.
   - `cli.ts`: `run --kit <file> --worktree <dg worktree>`. It reuses our `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` launch, vault lease and build delivery rather than copying them, then runs the `Machine`.
   - `hud.ts`: mounts Sid's controls bar and highlight ring in Obsidian and sends button presses back to Node, so step mode, case mode, pause, approve and flag all work.
   - Report output: `resultMarkdown` plus screenshots, ready for the PR body.
   - Out of scope for this first version: the SQL setup steps and the local proof database.
4. **Tests:** Vitest for the executor's action mapping and the HUD command bridge, following the repo's existing vitest setup.

**Verification:**
- **Stage 1:** run Sid's existing kit `eng-2176-obsidian.json` (7 cases; ENG-2176 is already merged as #1508) against a leased vault built from `discourse-graph` main. Pass bar:
  - the cases run
  - step and case pause work from the overlay
  - the copy-to-PR markdown and screenshots come out
- **Stage 2:** the change you actually want proved. I write a kit for that branch's Done When, plus regression cases, and run it against the branch build. Each case has a `decision` field, and you approve the kit before it runs.

**Risks I'll check early:**
- whether the button bridge from the overlay to Node survives a plugin reload
- whether the Settings window can be reached as a separate CDP target

If these fail, I'll fall back to a Node-only CLI that pauses in the terminal.

{"title":"Add link support to tldraw text shapes in Obsidian","description":"## Problem

* Text shapes cannot link to a page or URL, so a simplified canvas narrative cannot open the detailed source represented by its text.
* Geo shapes already provide this interaction, but text shapes do not.

## Solution

* Add the existing geo-shape link action and behavior to Obsidian text shapes.
* Reuse the geo-shape link code path instead of creating a separate text-shape implementation.

## Done When

* A text shape exposes the same **Edit link** action as a geo shape.
* A user can add, edit, open, and remove a link on a text shape with the same behavior and visual affordance as a geo shape.
* The link persists when the canvas is closed and reopened.
* Unit tests cover link persistence and the text-shape eligibility behavior.

## Out of Scope

* Converting a text shape into a Discourse Graph node.
* Adding a page picker or a new link format.
* Adding links to other unsupported shape types.

## Notes

* Child of <issue id="c3c3c16e-5ab2-469a-876d-36a4d9c9481d" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/FEE-907/alias-tldraw-canvas-elements-to-discourse-nodes">FEE-907</issue>.
* Obsidian counterpart to <issue id="7d8589fa-c286-404e-abd0-d39f7772aab6" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2227/add-link-support-to-tldraw-text-shapes-in-roam">ENG-2227</issue>.

Obsidian canvas scenarios driven over CDP (`dg-obsidian-cdp-verify`):

- Other sessions leave hidden canvas tabs open. `document.querySelector(".tl-canvas")` and `getLeavesOfType("tldraw-dg-preview")[0]` then hit the wrong canvas. Scope every query to `app.workspace.activeLeaf.view.containerEl`.

---

When `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` relaunches Obsidian (window ~1024 CSS px), both sidebars reopen and a canvas tab is only ~390px wide. tldraw then uses its narrow layout: no `.tlui-style-panel`, fixture shapes off-screen, drags silently create nothing (menu never opens, 0 arrows).

Fix in the scenario, not the vault: `app.workspace.leftSplit.collapse(); app.workspace.rightSplit.collapse();` before placing the camera. The harness restores the layout after each scenario. Place the camera from measured rects (style panel / container edges), not fixed camera coords, since widths vary by window. Related: [[reference_obsidian_cdp_driving]].
== reference_tldraw_store_put_no_listener
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: e9bb47d2-c844-4381-8d17-490ed7677aa5
  modified: 2026-09-14T15:38:17.782Z
---

A raw `store.put()` on the Obsidian canvas's `TLStore` (reachable over CDP as
`app.workspace.getLeavesOfType("tldraw-dg-preview")[0].view.store`) updates the store and
re-renders the shape, but **fires no `store.listen()` callbacks** — verified by registering a
listener with the same `{ source: "user", scope: "document" }` options the plugin uses and
counting 0 calls. The plugin's autosave hangs off that listener, so programmatic puts never
reach the markdown file and look like a persistence bug in whatever you just built.

Diagnose it by checking the *store* and the *file* separately over time: shape present in
store + absent from file, indefinitely, means the listener never fired — not that saving is broken.

Drive real input instead (`Input.dispatchMouseEvent` / `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` /
`Input.insertText`): select the tool, click to place, type, Escape. That exercises the editor,
flushes the reactor, and the 500 ms `DEFAULT_SAVE_DELAY` debounce then writes the file. Real
input is also the only way to test shape *creation*, which is where `getDefaultProps` bugs
surface.

Related gotchas found the same way:
- `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` rejects `text: undefined` — omit the key entirely on `keyUp` and for
  non-printable keys like Escape, or CDP returns `Invalid 'text' parameter`.
- Counting `.tl-shape` elements immediately after a store load reads 0 because React has not
  painted yet. Poll for the count instead of asserting once, or you will misread viewport
  culling / paint timing as a blank canvas.
- `document.elementFromPoint` at a shape's hyperlink icon returns `.tl-canvas`, not the anchor —
  for geo shapes too. tldraw hit-tests through its own canvas layer, so this is not evidence of a
  z-index bug. Always measure a stock shape type as a control before believing a rendering regression.

See [[reference-obsidian-cdp-driving]] for attaching to a vault over CDP.
== reference_cdp_verify_harness_contract
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: e9bb47d2-c844-4381-8d17-490ed7677aa5
  modified: 2026-09-30T03:55:15.916Z
---

Three contract details in `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify`'s scenario API. Getting them wrong fails every
scenario with the *same* error, which reads like a product bug rather than a harness mistake — on
ENG-2228 all five scenarios failed identically at "timeout waiting for text shape in store" when
the real cause was the driver calls.

- **`evaluate(expr)` wraps the body in a plain function and only adds a `return` when the string
  contains no `return` at all** (`driver.mjs`: `/\breturn\b/.test(expression) ? expression : "return (…)"`).
  So a self-invoking `(() => { … return x; })()` matches the regex, is treated as a *body*, and
  silently yields `undefined`. Always write an explicit top-level `return …;`.
- **`waitFor(expr)` resolves only when the expression evaluates to literal `true`.** It returns
  `undefined`, never the value. Use it for the condition, then a separate `evaluate` to read data —
  `await waitFor("return shapes.length > 0;")` then `await evaluate("return shapes[0].id;")`.
- **`key()` takes an options object, not a string.** `client.key("t")` spreads a string into the CDP
  params and does nothing; use
  `client.key({ text: "t", key: "t", code: "KeyT", windowsVirtualKeyCode: 84, nativeVirtualKeyCode: 84 })`.
  `typeText` and `pressEscape` are the string-friendly wrappers.

Other operational notes:

- Slots come from `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. A worktree created
  before that variable existed won't have it — copy the line from the main checkout's `.env`
  (it is gitignored, so it is not inherited). `doctor.mjs --slot N` tells you which vault resolves.
- The build mirrors to the slot's vault, which may not be the vault you have open. Check the
  `mirrored to …` line before assuming a stale build; see
  [[reference-obsidian-contested-vault-plugin-dir]].
- Flaky single failures are real here — a scenario that passed on the previous run with identical
  code usually passes again. Rerun before diagnosing, per the skill's own gotcha table.

Raw CDP driving without the harness: [[reference-obsidian-cdp-driving]]. Note that programmatic
`store.put` fires no tldraw store listeners, so it never triggers the canvas autosave —

content.content:
> **TL;DR** PR #1442 is open at `5253da0d` with the link stored in `shape.meta.url`
> and the icon drawn by a canvas overlay, after Michael asked us to compare against
> the original props-schema approach. CI green-ish and re-running; blocked on his
> re-review and on Trang's Loom. A delegated review found a real `obsidian://`
> bypass, now fixed.

## Goal / scope agreement

The ticket's instruction to "reuse the geo-shape link code path" rests on a **wrong
premise**: there is no app-side geo link code. The action, dialog and icon are all
stock tldraw 3.14.2, gated on the duck-type `'url' in shape.props`. So the work is a
storage + eligibility problem, not UI wiring. ENG-2227 reached the same conclusion on
the Roam side.

Agreed deviations from `Done When`, all stated in the PR body: `obsidian://` page-link
support (ticket lists "a new link format" as out of scope, but its Problem statement
names page links as the primary target and `T.linkUrl` cannot express one), click-gesture
alignment with discourse nodes, and a pnpm patch of tldraw. **Unit tests are explicitly
out at Trang's request**, which leaves the ticket's fourth `Done When` unmet.

## Approved plan
## Gotchas / landmines

- This worktree's `.env` files predate newer variables. `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` (apps/obsidian) and `DG_ROAM_PLAYWRIGHT_GRAPH_URL_1` / `_EMAIL_1` / `_PASSWORD_1` (apps/roam) had to be copied from the main checkout. **One copy corrupted `apps/roam/.env`** by appending onto a line with no trailing newline, gluing a key onto `BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN`'s value — repaired, backup at `apps/roam/.env.bak-eng2228`.
- `pnpm build` mirrors to the **slot** vault — here `testVault2`, not the `testVault` that was open. Check the `mirrored to …` line before concluding a build is stale.
- `address_comments: true` on the PR monitor would auto-reply to human reviewers, which contradicts the draft-first rule. Left off deliberately; `auto_fix` also left off.
- Michael's three inline threads are answered but still unresolved — only he can clear `CHANGES_REQUESTED`.

## Current state

Add the prefix obsidian-icon- before the Obsidian icon name.

These rules must be followed for the plugin to be accepted into the Obsidian community plugin store.

### Security

- Never use `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, or `insertAdjacentHTML` with user-controlled content

### App instance

- Always use `this.app` — never the global `app` object

### Event listeners

- Register all event listeners via `this.registerEvent()` so they are automatically cleaned up on plugin unload

### UI text

- Use sentence case in settings headings and labels (not title case)

### Commands

- Do not set default hotkeys — they conflict with other plugins

- Do not manually prepend the plugin ID to command IDs — Obsidian adds it automatically

### Workspace

- Do not store references to custom views — look them up fresh each time they are needed
  Don't do this:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => this.view = new MyCustomView());`
  Do this instead:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => new MyCustomView());`
  To access the view from your plugin, use `Workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType():`

```
for (let leaf of app.workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType(MY_VIEW_TYPE)) {
  let view = leaf.view;
  if (view instanceof MyCustomView) {
    // ...
  }
}
```

- Do not detach leaves during plugin unload

### Editor

- Prefer the Editor API over `Vault.modify()` when the note is currently open in the editor
- Prefer `Vault.process()` instead of `Vault.modify()` to modify a file in the background

### Mobile compatibility

- Node.js and Electron APIs (`fs`, `crypto`, `os`) are unavailable on mobile
- If the plugin targets mobile, use web API equivalents: `SubtleCrypto` instead of `crypto`, `navigator.clipboard` for clipboard access
- Regex lookbehind assertions are not supported on some mobile — avoid them if possible

- Use `const`/`let` — never `var`

- Minimize `console.log` — remove debug logs before shipping

Your watched run is up in Obsidian (`testVault2`):
- **Case 1** (text shape offers Edit link) passed.
- **Case 2** is paused at the case boundary, waiting for you.

**To drive it:**
- Use only the caption bar at the bottom of the Obsidian window. Clicking or typing on the canvas while it runs pauses the run, which is the overlay working as intended. That's also what upset the cursor steps earlier.
- Press the bar's continue button to start each next case. You can also use Pause / Flag / Cases, the pace menu, or `Ctrl+Alt+Space` (pause/resume) and `Ctrl+Alt+.` (next step).
- After case 8 the result sheet opens. Close it, and the runner writes `result.md` and exits.

When a "resumed" event shows up in the journal, that confirms your clicks reach the runner through the button bridge. I'll check for it when the run finishes.

**Status so far:**

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Runner | Lives in `~/Desktop/code/proof-kit`, branch `obsidian-runner`, uncommitted. 56/56 vitest pass, type-check clean |
| Stage 1: Sid's ENG-2176 kit | 5 of 6 pass. 1 left out because it needs the proof database |
| Stage 2: ENG-2228 kit, unattended | 8 of 8 pass, with no failed steps. Validator case rejected and kept in the kit |

**Two findings to pass on:**
- **Sid's ENG-2176 kit:** `[data-type="discourse-context-view"]` matches Obsidian's tab header before the view itself. The kit needs `.workspace-leaf-content[...]`.
- **ENG-2228 (PR #1442):** the link dialog's **Clear** button only appears when the field holds an *invalid* link. Removing a link means emptying the field and pressing **Save**. That comes from tldraw's dialog, which this one forks, but it could confuse users.

## plugin:claude-for-nonprofits:gmail
This is an MCP server provided by Gmail API. The server provides tools for developers to build LLM applications on top of Gmail.

## plugin:claude-for-nonprofits:google-calendar
This is an MCP server provided by Google Calendar API. The server provides tools for developers to build LLM applications on top of Calendar.

## plugin:claude-for-nonprofits:google-drive
This is an MCP server provided by Drive API. The server provides tools for developers to build LLM applications on top of Drive.

## plugin:claude-for-nonprofits:granted
Granted: live U.S. grant database (federal, state, and private foundation funding) for nonprofits, schools, government agencies, and small businesses. Call search_grants to discover live opportunities by topic or keyword, get_grant for full details by slug, search_funders/get_funder to research private foundations, and get_past_winners to find prior recipients of a federal program.

## plugin:claude-for-nonprofits:kindora

    Kindora — funder and nonprofit data for grant seekers and the people who help them.

    Data comes from public sources: IRS Form 990 filings and the IRS Business Master File,
    Canada's CRA charity filings and register, the Charity Commission for England and Wales,
    OSCR, the ACNC, Kenya's NGO board, 360Giving (UK), IATI, organizations' and funders' own
    websites, job boards, and government grant listings. Every tool only reads, except
    start_kindora_profile and start_connect_profile.

    TOOLS:
    - search_funders: grantmaking organizations by name, topic, or location
    - search_open_grants: open grant opportunities and RFPs by topic, cause area, or keywords
    - search_funder_jobs: open jobs at foundations (program officers, grants managers, CEOs)
    - search_nonprofits: the recipient side — nonprofits by cause, place, size, or funding
      received; `thesis` ranks them by a plain-language description
    - find_funders_of_nonprofit: who has funded one named nonprofit
    - search_organizations: nonprofits, NGOs and social enterprises in every country Kindora
      holds (US, Canada, UK, Australia, Kenya and more), by name, topic, country and role
    - get_organization_profile: one organization's full research profile: registrations,

Use it for anything to do with finding, choosing, inviting or welcoming members of a board, advisory committee, community of practice or similar group, such as a skills matrix, working out what the board is missing, deciding what to ask of members, thinking through someone they have in mind, or writing an invitation. Use it even if they only mention open seats or terms ending. Not for hiring staff, recruiting volunteers or running board meetings.

Use when someone has a goal to reach people by a date ("we need to raise $45k by June") or an event or drive to fill ("help me plan our fundraiser," "we need more volunteers"), even if they never say "campaign." Also use when they ask how a campaign is going or what to change in the time left, when it's over and they want to know what worked, or when they need a send calendar or a list of what to track. Not for writing or reviewing a single email or post, or for plans that aren't campaigns. Use it whether they want a few quick ideas or a full plan; when that's unclear, it starts by asking.
- claude-for-nonprofits:content-review: Helps nonprofits and funders check a piece before it goes out under the organization's name. Use it when the user shares or pastes a draft meant for people outside the organization, such as an appeal, email, newsletter, social post, invite, flyer, thank-you, press release or grant announcement, and asks for a look, a reaction, a re-check or a fix, or asks if a line in it is OK to say. Read it before you review, fix, shorten or rewrite the piece, so the piece doesn't put anyone at risk or say something the organization can't support. Do not use it for writing something new, for a general tax or legal question with no piece, or for contracts, grant reports, 990s and internal documents.
- claude-for-nonprofits:deck-planning: Helps nonprofits and funders plan and make decks that only say things the organization can support. Use it for updates, donor newsletter pieces, one appeal, a reply to a funder's no and news of a delay. Use it to prepare for or write up a meeting with a donor, a foundation, a company, an embassy, a government or UN agency, or anyone else who might fund the work. - claude-for-nonprofits:funder-and-grant-research: Read this before you answer any question about finding or researching a funder, a grant or a person who might give. It covers what's OK to look up about a person and how to cite sources. Use it for any question about who gives money to a cause ("who could fund our after-school program?", "find grants for our food pantry", "who gives to animal shelters around here?"), including finding new individual donors. Use it to look up a named foundation, company, agency or person (who they are, what they fund and how to apply). Use it when someone pastes or shares a grant call or funding notice, even with only "thoughts?" or "FYI" and even when the deadline has passed. Not for working with a funder or donor they already have (renewals, staying in touch, meeting prep, thank-yous, appeals), writing applications, reports owed to funders or campaign plans.

Use it when someone shares a funder's call or guidelines and wants to start, needs an answer cut to a word or character limit, or wants last year's proposal turned into one for a new funder. Not for finding funders or deciding whether to apply, reports on a grant already won, or thank-yous, updates, appeals and first emails to donors and sponsors.
- claude-for-nonprofits:grant-reporting: Read this before you help with a report to a funder or a newly won grant. It covers how to report results honestly and how to protect the people in a report. Use it when someone says they won, got or were awarded a grant, even if they only share the news ("we just got the county grant!"), when they share an award letter or grant agreement, and when they ask what they owe a funder or what's due on their grants. Not for applying for a grant, finding funders, thank-yous, informal updates or meeting prep with a funder, or an annual report for the public.
- claude-for-nonprofits:hr-policy-lookup: Read this before you answer any question about what staff or volunteers at the user's organization are entitled to, allowed to do or have to do, even if it doesn't mention a policy. It might be a lookup or a request for advice ("can I keep this gift?", "who do I report this to?", "how should I log these hours?", "how long do we keep records?", "is our policy legal?"). Common topics are leave, benefits, expenses, gifts from clients, volunteer paperwork and timesheets for grants. Use it even if you know what's usual. People will rely on the answer, so it has to come from their own policy. Read it before you open or answer from their handbook, a policy or a memo, or a grant agreement that comes with a question about a cost. Not for questions about the law alone, the AI use policy, writing policies, onboarding plans or performance reviews.
- claude-for-nonprofits:job-post-builder: Writes the hiring documents for a nonprofit or funder, for a paid or volunteer role. Open this skill for any request to write a job post or job description, interview questions or an interview guide, a screening rubric, an offer letter or a volunteer role description, even a one-line request with no details, before asking the user anything ("write interview questions for a case manager," "draft an offer letter," "help me hire a development director"). Open it when a role is open, new or grant-funded, or when someone is leaving, has left or needs replacing, and nobody is hired for it yet ("we need to replace our office manager," "our grant funds a new case manager"), and when interviews are coming up ("my interviews start Monday"). Open it when someone asks to screen, rank, compare, score or reject real applicants or resumes. It judges no applicant, and gives a rubric to use. Not for a person already hired or with a start date, which is onboarding, nor for recruiting board members or someone's own resume.
- claude-for-nonprofits:new-hire-onboarding: Makes any part of onboarding for a staff member who has been hired or has accepted an offer at a nonprofit or funder, such as a pre-start or first-day checklist, a first-week plan, 30/60/90-day goals, a welcome message, a who-to-ask list, or the whole plan. Open it first, before asking questions or drafting, for any request to make one of these, however brief ("write a welcome message for our new development associate," "make a checklist for our new coordinator's first day"), for any question about what a new person's first day or week should hold ("what should our new hire do in their first week?"), and for any remark about someone just hired, with or without a job title ("our new hire starts Monday," "we have a new employee joining," "we just hired a youth mentor"). Not for a role that is still to be filled, or is being created or funded with nobody hired yet, which is job-post-builder's. Not for volunteers, board members, offer letters, handbook questions or performance reviews.
- claude-for-nonprofits:org-voice-guide: Keeps a nonprofit writing in one shared voice, the organization's. It has two jobs. (1) Writing in that voice. Read it before you write anything short that the public will read under the organization's name and that no other skill covers, such as a social post, a caption, a blurb, web copy or a flyer. Open it even for a one-line request you could just write, because the organization may have a voice guide that you can't see until you look. Use it too when a draft reads as corporate, generic or not like them. (2) The guide itself. Use it when someone wants to set up, find, follow, change or share their organization's brand voice or style guide ("get Claude to write like us", "our comms lead has a style guide, can you follow it"). That includes a one-word change ("we call them members now", "we stopped saying clients"), even when it looks like a quick memory edit, because the old word has to be recorded as one to avoid. Not for personal writing, such as a note to a coworker, and not for logos or visual design.
- claude-for-nonprofits:where-things-live: Helps organizations map where each kind of their data lives. Use it when the user asks about data related to donors and gifts, funders and grants, finance, official documents and policies, board and governance, programs and the people served, staff and volunteers, communications and marketing, day-to-day work, or events. Read it before you search for, open, count, summarize, organize or connect any of the organization's own files, records, folders or tools, so you look in the right place first and can offer the map afterwards. Also use it if the user asks more generally about where their data lives, how to set Claude up for their organization, or how to map their data. Do not use when another Claude for Nonprofits skill might trigger, such as writing a grant report or a thank-you note.
- mattpocock-skills:pr: Use when writing a PR body.

Common topics are leave, benefits, expenses, gifts from clients, volunteer paperwork and timesheets for grants. Use it even if you know what's usual. People will rely on the answer, so it has to come from their own policy. Read it before you open or answer from their handbook, a policy or a memo, or a grant agreement that comes with a question about a cost. Not for questions about the law alone, the AI use policy, writing policies, onboarding plans or performance reviews.
- claude-for-nonprofits:job-post-builder: Writes the hiring documents for a nonprofit or funder, for a paid or volunteer role. Open this skill for any request to write a job post or job description, interview questions or an interview guide, a screening rubric, an offer letter or a volunteer role description, even a one-line request with no details, before asking the user anything ("write interview questions for a case manager," "draft an offer letter," "help me hire a development director"). Open it when a role is open, new or grant-funded, or when someone is leaving, has left or needs replacing, and nobody is hired for it yet ("we need to replace our office manager," "our grant funds a new case manager"), and when interviews are coming up ("my interviews start Monday"). Open it when someone asks to screen, rank, compare, score or reject real applicants or resumes. It judges no applicant, and gives a rubric to use. Not for a person already hired or with a start date, which is onboarding, nor for recruiting board members or someone's own resume.
- claude-for-nonprofits:new-hire-onboarding: Makes any part of onboarding for a staff member who has been hired or has accepted an offer at a nonprofit or funder, such as a pre-start or first-day checklist, a first-week plan, 30/60/90-day goals, a welcome message, a who-to-ask list, or the whole plan. Open it first, before asking questions or drafting, for any request to make one of these, however brief ("write a welcome message for our new development associate," "make a checklist for our new coordinator's first day"), for any question about what a new person's first day or week should hold ("what should our new hire do in their first week?"), and for any remark about someone just hired, with or without a job title ("our new hire starts Monday," "we have a new employee joining," "we just hired a youth mentor"). Not for a role that is still to be filled, or is being created or funded with nobody hired yet, which is job-post-builder's. Not for volunteers, board members, offer letters, handbook questions or performance reviews.
- claude-for-nonprofits:org-voice-guide: Keeps a nonprofit writing in one shared voice, the organization's. It has two jobs. (1) Writing in that voice. Read it before you write anything short that the public will read under the organization's name and that no other skill covers, such as a social post, a caption, a blurb, web copy or a flyer. Open it even for a one-line request you could just write, because the organization may have a voice guide that you can't see until you look. Use it when someone wants to set up, find, follow, change or share their organization's brand voice or style guide ("get Claude to write like us", "our comms lead has a style guide, can you follow it"). Not for personal writing, such as a note to a coworker, and not for logos or visual design.

Use it when the user asks about data related to donors and gifts, funders and grants, finance, official documents and policies, board and governance, programs and the people served, staff and volunteers, communications and marketing, day-to-day work, or events. Read it before you search for, open, count, summarize, organize or connect any of the organization's own files, records, folders or tools, so you look in the right place first and can offer the map afterwards. Also use it if the user asks more generally about where their data lives, how to set Claude up for their organization, or how to map their data. - [reference_obsidian_escape_keymap_scope.md](reference_obsidian_escape_keymap_scope.md) — Escape in an Obsidian Modal can't be stopped from the DOM; push a keymap scope
- [reference_tailwind_arbitrary_shadow_var.md](reference_tailwind_arbitrary_shadow_var.md) — shadow-[var(--x)] is inert in Tailwind; needs the shadow: type hint
- [feedback_explain_moved_code_inline.md](feedback_explain_moved_code_inline.md) — On big deletions, leave an inline PR comment saying where the code moved
- [reference_scope_context_provider_to_avoid_reindent.md](reference_scope_context_provider_to_avoid_reindent.md) — Scope context providers to the smallest consuming subtree; wrapping a big JSX tree makes Prettier reindent everything
- [project_settings_overhaul_stack.md](project_settings_overhaul_stack.md) — Settings overhaul is one stacked branch chain; ENG-2184 sits above ENG-2189 despite Linear's ordering note
- [reference_reviewdog_fails_on_warnings.md](reference_reviewdog_fails_on_warnings.md) — CI lint-changed-files fails on ESLint *warnings* for added lines; local lint exits 0
- [reference_obsidian_orphaned_relation_types.md](reference_obsidian_orphaned_relation_types.md) — Deleting a relation type orphans its relations in relations.json; the panel hides them, so counts must filter by configured type
- [reference_cm6_widget_ignore_event.md](reference_cm6_widget_ignore_event.md) — CM6 WidgetType.ignoreEvent() defaults to true and that's what clickable widgets want; false breaks their click handler
- [reference_cm6_decorations_not_dom_stamping.md](reference_cm6_decorations_not_dom_stamping.md) — Style CM-owned spans with CM6 decorations, never MutationObserver stamping; CM recreates them on focus and scroll
- [reference_turbo_cache_masks_failures.md](reference_turbo_cache_masks_failures.md) — ci:validate can exit 0 on a stale turbo cache; --force to baseline, but a local failure may just be a stale node_modules — let CI decide
- [feedback_pnpm_add_lockfile_churn.md](feedback_pnpm_add_lockfile_churn.md) — pnpm add and patch-commit rewrite files you didn't touch (patch-commit strips pnpm-workspace.yaml comments); hand-edit + plain pnpm install
- [reference_obsidian_contested_vault_plugin_dir.md](reference_obsidian_contested_vault_plugin_dir.md) — Another worktree's dev watcher silently overwrote the vault plugin build mid-verification; grep the bundle for a symbol you just added
- [reference_roam_ext_dev_symlink_contested.md](reference_roam_ext_dev_symlink_contested.md) — ~/roam-ext-dev is shared across worktree sessions; check its target before trusting a Roam reload
- [reference_launch_json_resolves_to_main_repo.md](reference_launch_json_resolves_to_main_repo.md) — preview_start reads the MAIN repo's .claude/launch.json; add a per-worktree entry on its own port
- [reference_tailwind_preflight_disabled_obsidian.md](reference_tailwind_preflight_disabled_obsidian.md) — Tailwind transform/filter/ring/shadow utilities are inert in apps/obsidian (no preflight); use an arbitrary property. Side borders need border-0 border-r border-solid
- [reference_create_pr_target_branch_drift.md](reference_create_pr_target_branch_drift.md) — /create-pr's Target branch comes from the main checkout, not the session's worktree; verify before pushing
- [reference_tldraw_store_put_no_listener.md](reference_tldraw_store_put_no_listener.md) — tldraw store.listen ignores programmatic store.put, so CDP puts never autosave; drive real input events
- [reference_agents_skills_not_discovered.md](reference_agents_skills_not_discovered.md) — Claude Code never scans .agents/skills; symlink into .claude/skills and ~/.claude/skills
- [feedback_enforcement_hierarchy_over_prose_rules.md](feedback_enforcement_hierarchy_over_prose_rules.md) — A rule a linter already catches should not cost AGENTS.md budget; reviewdog makes new eslint rules free to adopt
- [reference_tldraw_schema_fallback.md](reference_tldraw_schema_fallback.md) — tldraw migrations run at load only; schema-less files need current schema minus your own sequence ids
- [reference_roam_ships_tailwind2.md](reference_roam_ships_tailwind2.md) — Roam ships pre-JIT Tailwind 2 with no preflight: arbitrary values inert, borders need border-0 border-solid, 1rem = 14px
- [reference_obsidian_parseyaml_semantics.md](reference_obsidian_parseyaml_semantics.md) — Obsidian parseYaml is the `yaml` package, not js-yaml; diverges from gray-matter on dates/octal/malformed
- [reference_github_graphql_bot_login.md](reference_github_graphql_bot_login.md) — GraphQL drops the [bot] suffix from bot logins; filter on author.__typename
- [reference_obsidian_markdownrenderer_section_mapping.md](reference_obsidian_markdownrenderer_section_mapping.md) — MarkdownRenderer.render emits one top-level element per cache section (footnotes/EOF exceptions); map line → DOM by section index
- [reference_pr_evidence_worktree_roam_profile.md](reference_pr_evidence_worktree_roam_profile.md) — pr-evidence in a new worktree: point DG_ROAM_PLAYWRIGHT_PROFILE_DIR_1 at the main checkout's signed-in Roam profile
- [reference_pr_evidence_roam_login.md](reference_pr_evidence_roam_login.md) — pr-evidence needs the worktree's Playwright profile signed in (auto-login off); Chrome upload path can't return tokened URLs
- [External comms pattern](feedback_external_comms_pattern.md) — Trang’s comment structure: @stakeholders, numbered claims, current state → problem → suggestion, → chains, end with one question
- [Commit unit tests](feedback_commit_unit_tests.md) — apps/obsidian has Vitest; commit tests for new helpers in src/**/__tests__/, CDP scenarios stay in the scratchpad
- [reference_obsidian_settings_separate_window.md](reference_obsidian_settings_separate_window.md) — Obsidian 1.13 Settings is a separate window; CDP mouse can't reach it, drive via activeTab.containerEl DOM
- [reference_obsidian_cdp_canvas_narrow_breakpoint.md](reference_obsidian_cdp_canvas_narrow_breakpoint.md) — CDP canvas scenarios: open sidebars push tldraw below its breakpoint (no style panel); collapse them and place camera from measured rects
- [reference_cm6_mark_cannot_wrap_obsidian_hashtag.md](reference_cm6_mark_cannot_wrap_obsidian_hashtag.md) — Prec.highest can't make a mark wrap .cm-hashtag; colour the chip via mark CSS vars + ::before
- [reference_obsidian_modal_overflow_clips_popovers.md](reference_obsidian_modal_overflow_clips_popovers.md) — .modal is overflow:auto; absolute dropdowns in short modals clip and clicks close the modal — add overflow-visible
- [reference_cdp_verify_harness_contract.md](reference_cdp_verify_harness_contract.md) — dg-obsidian-cdp-verify: evaluate() needs explicit return, waitFor() needs literal true, key() takes an object
- [feedback_draft_review_replies_first.md](feedback_draft_review_replies_first.md) — Never post replies to a human reviewer directly; draft in chat and wait for approval
- [reference_cdp_tldraw_editor_and_active_leaf.md](reference_cdp_tldraw_editor_and_active_leaf.md) — CDP canvas: scope to activeLeaf, editor via fiber from .tl-canvas, DiscourseToolPanel reuses .tlui-style-panel
- [reference_roam_loader_canvas_driving.md](reference_roam_loader_canvas_driving.md) — Driving the Roam canvas via playwright:load-extension: dev build for tldrawApps, close the settings dialog, centre the camera, prove the menu opened
- [reference_obsidian_vault_leases.md](reference_obsidian_vault_leases.md) — Obsidian vaults are leased per worktree via the obsidian-vault skill; start watchers with vault.mjs dev, ask before --take
- [reference_pr_evidence_camo_broken.md](reference_pr_evidence_camo_broken.md) — Roam file.upload serves octet-stream, so pr-evidence URLs fail GitHub camo (400) and don't render inline; still fine as download links
- [reference_blueprint_popover_escape_closes_dialog.md](reference_blueprint_popover_escape_closes_dialog.md) — Escape in a Popover inside a Blueprint Dialog closes the Dialog; stopPropagation in the popover content
- [reference_roam_jsdom_no_css_escape.md](reference_roam_jsdom_no_css_escape.md) — apps/roam jsdom has no CSS.escape; match block uids by dataset equality, skip embeds, scope to container
- [reference_roam_relation_type_identity.md](reference_roam_relation_type_identity.md) — Roam relation "types" are derived from triplets; identity is label + complement, never label alone
- [reference_obsidian_watcher_ignores_css.md](reference_obsidian_watcher_ignores_css.md) — Obsidian dev watcher never rebuilds on CSS-only edits; run a NODE_ENV=development build.ts and grep the vault styles.css
- [reference_roam_test_graph_stored_relations_off.md](reference_roam_test_graph_stored_relations_off.md) — Slot-1 test graph has stored relations off; use "Reactivate without Migration", Deactivate in cleanup; loader page error is environmental
- [reference_chromium_focus_visible_inherits_from_input.md](reference_chromium_focus_visible_inherits_from_input.md) — Script focus from a focused text input inherits :focus-visible; pointer-opened menus should focus the panel, keyboard opens the item
- [reference_roam_dev_extension_needs_depot_refresh.md](reference_roam_dev_extension_needs_depot_refresh.md) — Page reload keeps the old dev extension; refresh `dist` in Settings → Roam Depot → Developer Extensions and prove it with a changed behaviour
- [reference_roam_loader_assert_build_stamp.md](reference_roam_loader_assert_build_stamp.md) — Shared slot-1 graph can run another session's DG build; assert the settings version stamp names your branch in each load-extension test
- [feedback_frequent_manual_test_pauses.md](feedback_frequent_manual_test_pauses.md) — UI feature work: ship small slices and pause for Trang to test each by hand, with exact steps

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions. Claude publishes an artifact for apps, sites, dashboards and games, and whenever the person asks for an artifact or for an HTML or Markdown page to view or share. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. A page declares these through the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of this would make the page more useful, Claude must load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code.** Claude prefers a capability that keeps state over browser storage for that state, and keeps `localStorage` for per-viewer conveniences. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. The one exception is a workshop document from the `workshop` skill, which carries its own design: there Claude skips `artifact-design` and loads `artifact-diagramming` for a template page's diagrams. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com or cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/ (the skill has the full list) and stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Claude always authors the page as `.html`, and publishes a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly asks for one. When the person shares a Markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, Claude builds an HTML page from its content, keeping its substance and designing the page as it would any other artifact rather than transcribing the Markdown one to one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB work, but each artifact has its own origin and what a page stores lives only in that viewer's browser. It survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices or Claude. It can come back empty, or the accessor can throw, in a private window, with cleared or blocked site data, in previews or during thumbnail capture, so Claude wraps every read and write in try/catch and makes the page render correctly without it.
