[Pricing on Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/pricing) — Learn about Vercel's pricing model, including the resources and services that are billed, and how they are priced. - [Vercel Storage overview](https://vercel.com/docs/storage) — Store files with Vercel Blob, runtime configuration with Global Config, and application data with Marketplace databases. - [Limits and Pricing for Image Optimization](https://vercel.com/docs/image-optimization/limits-and-pricing) — This page outlines information on the limits that are applicable when using Image Optimization, and the costs they can i - [Manage and optimize usage](https://vercel.com/docs/pricing/manage-and-optimize-usage) — Understand how to manage and optimize your usage on Vercel, learn how to track your usage, set up alerts, and optimize y Full cross-link map for this page: [/docs/vercel-blob/usage-and-pricing.graph.md](/docs/vercel-blob/usage-and-pricing.graph.md) - **Storage Size**: Monthly average of your blob store size (GB-month) - **Simple Operations**: Counts when a blob is accessed by its URL and it's a cache MISS, or when you retrieve blob metadata without downloading the blob - **Advanced Operations**: Counts when you upload, copy, or list blobs, and when you create a Blob store - **Blob Data Transfer**: Charged when blobs are downloaded or viewed - **[CDN Requests](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#cdn-requests)**: Each blob access by its URL counts as one CDN Request, regardless if it's a MISS or HIT - **[Fast Origin Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-origin-transfer)**: Applied only for cache MISS scenarios See the [usage details](#usage-details) and [pricing example](#pricing-example) sections for more information on how usage is calculated. > **💡 Note:** Stored files are referred to as "blobs" once they're in the storage system, > following cloud storage terminology. ## Pricing | Resource | Price | Included (Pro) | Included (Hobby) | |----------|-------|----------------|-----------------| | [Blob Storage Size](/docs/vercel-blob/usage-and-pricing#pricing) | Regional | Usage-based | 1GB/month | | [Blob Simple Operations](/docs/vercel-blob/usage-and-pricing#pricing) | Regional | Usage-based | First 10,000 | | [Blob Advanced Operations](/docs/vercel-blob/usage-and-pricing#pricing) | Regional | Usage-based | First 2,000 | | [Blob Data Transfer](/docs/vercel-blob/usage-and-pricing#pricing) | Regional | Flat Rate CDN | First 10 GB |
> **💡 Note:** [CDN Requests](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#cdn-requests) and [Fast Origin > Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-origin-transfer) for blobs are billed > at standard [CDN rates](/docs/cdn#pricing-and-usage). The included resource usage for > the Hobby plan is shared across all Vercel services in your project. ## Usage details - Cache HITs do not count as Simple Operations - Cache HITs do not incur Fast Origin Transfer charges - The maximum size of a blob in cache is [512 MB](/docs/vercel-blob/usage-and-pricing#size-limits). Any blob larger than this will generate a cache MISS on every access, resulting in a Fast Origin Transfer and CDN Request charge each time it is accessed - Uploads do not incur data transfer charges when using [Client Uploads](/docs/vercel-blob/client-upload) - Uploads incur [Fast Data Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-data-transfer) charges when using [Server Uploads](/docs/vercel-blob/server-upload) if your Vercel application is the one receiving the file upload - [Multipart uploads](/docs/vercel-blob#multipart-uploads) count as multiple Advanced Operations: one when starting, one per part, one for completion - Creating a Blob store counts as one Advanced Operation; deleting a store is free - Delete operations are free - **Dashboard interactions count as operations**: Each time you interact with the Vercel dashboard to browse your blob store, upload files, or view blob details, these actions count as Advanced Operations and will appear in your usage metrics. ## Private and public storage delivery costs Private and public Blob stores are priced the same for storage, operations, and uploads. The difference is in how files are delivered, which affects data transfer costs. **Private blob delivery** (e.g. a 10 KB document served through a [Function](/docs/functions)): - Your Function fetches the blob from the store, then streams it to the browser - You pay [Blob Data Transfer](/docs/vercel-blob#blob-data-transfer) + [Fast Origin Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-origin-transfer) on cache miss for the Function-to-store fetch, plus [Fast Data Transfer](/docs/cdn) + [Fast Origin Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-origin-transfer) for the Function-to-browser response **Public blob delivery** (e.g. a 150 KB image on a page): - The browser fetches the blob directly from the store - You pay [Blob Data Transfer](/docs/vercel-blob#blob-data-transfer) + [Fast Origin Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-origin-transfer) on cache miss - Blob Data Transfer (BDT) is 3x more cost-efficient than Fast Data Transfer (FDT) on average For full details on how delivery works, see [delivering private blobs](/docs/vercel-blob/private-storage#delivering-private-blobs) and [delivering public blobs](/docs/vercel-blob/public-storage#delivering-public-blobs). ## Hobby Vercel Blob is free for Hobby users within the [usage limits](#pricing). Vercel will send you emails as you are nearing your usage limits. You **will not pay for any additional usage**. However, you will not be able to access Vercel Blob if limits are exceeded. In this scenario, you will have to wait until 30 days have passed before using Blob storage again. To remove these limits, you can start a Pro trial using the button below. ## Pro You pay for usage using your [monthly credit](/docs/plans/pro-plan#monthly-credit), which switches to on-demand once you have used it. Pro teams can [set up Spend Management](/docs/spend-management#managing-your-spend-amount) to get notified or to automatically take action, such as [using a webhook](/docs/spend-management#configuring-a-webhook) or pausing your projects when your usage hits a set spend amount. ## Enterprise Vercel Blob Enterprise pricing is custom. Contact your account team for contracted rates and support questions. ## Pricing Example Let's say during one month of usage, you upload 120,000 blobs of which 30% (36,000 blobs) are uploaded using multipart uploads with 5 parts each. Your storage averages 50 GB and your blobs are downloaded 2.5 million times, with a 70% cache HIT ratio (meaning 30% or 750,000 downloads are cache MISSes), for a total of 350 GB of data transfer. Here's the cost breakdown: - **Storage**: 50 GB total at $0.023/GB = $1.15 - **Simple Operations**: 750K (30% cache MISSes of 2.5M downloads + head calls) at $0.40/1M = $0.30 - **Advanced Operations**: - Single uploads: 84K (70% of 120K blobs) - Multipart uploads: 36K × (1 start + 5 parts + 1 completion) = 252K operations - Total: 336K at $5.00/1M = $1.68 - **Data Transfer** (iad1): 350 GB total at $0.05/GB = $17.50 - **CDN Requests**: 2.5M requests (all downloads) - 10M included = $0.00 - **Fast Origin Transfer** (iad1): 105 GB (30% cache MISSes of 350 GB) at $0.06/GB = $6.30 **Total**: $26.93/month ## Limits Vercel Blob has certain [limits](/docs/limits) that you should be aware of when designing your application. ### Store limits You can create as many Blob stores as you need. Creating a store counts as one [Advanced Operation](#usage). Deleting a store is free. You pay for storage, operations, and data transfer based on what you use. Splitting the same data across more stores doesn't change those costs. Use separate stores to isolate projects, environments, customers, or public and private content. ### Operation rate limits | Plan | Simple Operations | Advanced Operations | | ---------- | ----------------- | ------------------- | | Hobby | 1,200/min (20/s) | 900/min (15/s) | | Pro | 7,200/min (120/s) | 4,500/min (75/s) | | Enterprise | 9,000/min (150/s) | 7,500/min (125/s) | **Note:** Rate limits are based on the number of operations, not HTTP requests. For example, when using `del([pathnames])` to delete multiple blobs in one call, each blob deletion counts as a separate operation toward your rate limit. Deleting 100 blobs in a batch counts as 100 operations, not one. ### Size limits - **Cache Size Limit**: 512 MB per blob - Blobs larger than 512 MB will not be cached - Accessing these blobs will always count as a cache MISS (generating one [Simple Operation](/docs/vercel-blob#simple-operations)) - These large blobs will also incur [Fast Origin Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-origin-transfer) charges for each access - **Maximum File Size**: 5TB (5,000GB) - This is the absolute maximum size for any individual file uploaded to Vercel Blob - For files larger than 100MB, we recommend using [multipart uploads](/docs/vercel-blob#multipart-uploads) ## Observability You can monitor and analyze your Vercel Blob usage with the [Observability section in the sidebar](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F~%2Fobservability%2Fblob\&title=Go+to+Blob+Observability) in the Vercel Dashboard. --- [View full sitemap](/docs/sitemap) If you find anything wrong or missing or can't find something, submit feedback by reading https://vercel.com/feedback.md to improve Vercel.

lastPrompt: What's the cost of having Vercel blob for each PR?

content.text:
Short answer: about **4 cents per PR** with full traces, under a cent with slimmed traces. The real constraint is the plan's included quota, not the per-PR price.

**Vercel's published rates** (docs updated 2026-09-23; these are the `iad1` example rates, prices vary slightly by region, and I don't know our store's region):

| What | Rate |
|---|---|
| Storage | $0.023 per GB-month |
| Downloads (data transfer) | $0.05/GB, plus $0.06/GB the first time a file is fetched (cache miss) |
| Uploads, lists, copies | $5 per million operations |
| Reads that miss the cache | $0.40 per million |
| Uploads from a local CLI or CI | no transfer charge; only the operation count |
| Deletes | free |

**One PR, assuming 3 published runs and reviewers opening the latest trace 6 times:**

| | Full trace (76 MB, what we produced) | Slimmed trace (no filmstrip, ~8 MB, *my estimate, not measured*) |
|---|---|---|
| Storage, 3 runs | 0.23 GB → **$0.005/month** while kept | **$0.0006/month** |
| Uploads (~10 files per run) | **$0.0002** | same |
| Reviewers viewing (6 × 1 trace) | 0.46 GB → **~$0.03** | **~$0.003** |
| **Total, first month** | **~$0.04** | **< $0.01** |

**At team scale, say 100 PRs a month:**
- Full traces: about **$4/month** in viewing.
- Storage grows about 23 GB a year without cleanup, which is about $0.50/month after a year.
- Deleting runs older than 90 days caps storage around 7 GB, which is about $0.16/month. Deletes are free.
- Slimmed traces cut all of this by about 10×.

**The catch is the plan's included quota.**
- **Hobby:** includes only **1 GB of storage and 10 GB of transfer** a month, then Blob stops working for 30 days rather than charging. That's about 13 full traces, and the store is shared with the Roam PR builds that already publish there. Full traces would break that quickly; slimmed traces plus 90-day cleanup would fit.
- **Pro:** it all comes out of the $20 monthly credit, so it's effectively free at these numbers.

Which Vercel plan is the DiscourseGraphs team on? If it's Hobby, I'd publish slimmed traces and add 90-day cleanup from the start, or create a separate store so this can't take down Roam PR builds when it runs out.

Going with option A. Plan:
1. **The runner writes a `run.json`** with build, commit, timing and verdicts, so publishing doesn't have to reverse-engineer the result text.
2. **A `proof publish` command** uploads a run to `releases/proof/runs/<kit>/<run>/` (the trace, results and the kit) and updates `releases/proof/manifest.json`. A `--local <dir>` mode writes exactly the same layout to disk so we can test without publishing anything.
3. **The catalog page** is a single static `index.html`, organised app → kit → case, with status badges, the run history and an "Open trace" link per run.
4. **The trace viewer is self-hosted** under `releases/proof/viewer/`, copied from `playwright-core`.
5. **A safety check:** before uploading, publish scans the trace's network log for auth headers (cookies, API keys, `Authorization`) and refuses if it finds any.

I'll test everything locally first. Uploading to the public store waits for your explicit OK.

The steps are now part of the catalog page itself. Pick a case and every step is right there with its Before and After screens; nothing opens a separate page. The screenshot shows case 2, step 9 "save the link". Before: the link dialog filled in, with a red circle on Save where it clicked. After: the dialog is closed and the link icon sits beside the text.

**How it works on the page:**
- **Left sidebar:** every case, with a pass/fail dot. Rejected cases stay listed, struck through.
- **Case page:** the step list on one side, Before | After screenshots on the other. Click a step, or one of its actions (e.g. "Type 'obsidian://…'"), to see that moment. Click a screenshot to enlarge it.
- **◀ Play ▶,** or the ← → and Space keys. Play keeps going into the next case, so someone can watch the whole kit without clicking.
- **Run picker:** appears once a kit has more than one run, to compare an older run with today's.
- **Full trace:** Playwright's viewer is still linked under History as an optional deep dive (DOM, network, console). You never need it to review.

**How it's built:** `publish` cuts the screenshots out of the trace when it uploads.
- Before is the last frame before the action. After is the last frame before the next action starts, so the UI has settled.
- It uploads only the frames it uses: **4.1 MB for this run, against 75 MB for the full trace**.

**Checked** in headless Chromium at 1500 px in dark mode:
- Selecting a step works, as do the arrow keys.
- Play carried on from case 2 into case 3.
- No console errors. 70/70 unit tests pass, including a new one for how frames are picked.

**Ready to publish.** One choice first, since the store is public:
- **Walkthrough only (recommended):** about 4 MB, screenshots of the test vault. The full-trace link is left out.
- **Walkthrough plus full trace:** about 79 MB. The trace also holds the DOM of the whole Obsidian window, console logs and the remaining network calls. These are cleaned as described before, but there's more vault detail in them (file names, settings panels).

content.text:
## Where ENG-2369 stands

**The goal:** a repeatable way to decide which end-to-end tests a change needs, both acceptance (the Done When works) and regression (existing features still work). A person approves each test, and reviewers can step through the results instead of watching video. It should work for Roam, Obsidian and the database, not just Obsidian.

## Options we explored

**1. How to generate the test list**

| Explored | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Cursor's feature maps, gstack's `/plan-eng-review`, Playwright's test agents, BMAD's test-architecture module, Qodo, Autonoma, TestSprite, Spec Kit, Kiro | None both proposes cases from a diff and has a person approve each one. We borrowed their best parts |
| **Sid's `qa.ts`**, his generator in the proof kit | Not on GitHub; it lives only in a local folder on Sid's machine (`dg-demo-videos/proof`). Its output is visible in his kits and in PR #1581's proof report |
| **Our own `propose.ts`** | **Built.** A fresh agent given only its prompt proposed 8 cases for ENG-2228, and caught two regressions my hand-written kit missed |

**2. How to run the tests**

| Explored | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Sid's proof-runner (PR #26), whose engine works for any app | **Adopted.** I ported it to Obsidian with a CDP executor plus Sid's caption bar inside Obsidian |
| TesterArmy (e2e.tester.army) | Doesn't fit: no Electron support, no approval step, and the hosted product can't load our local builds. Two ideas worth borrowing: replaying recorded steps, and picking tests from the diff |
| Storybook | Can't run the host apps. We kept its layout ideas only |

**3. How reviewers see results**

| Explored | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Sid's videos | You prefer stepping through to watching |
| Playwright trace viewer | Works for Obsidian over CDP, but it opens as a separate app and the trace is 75 MB |
| Claude Artifact, Storybook, Playwright HTML report, hosted dashboards | Compared; none chosen |
| **One catalog page with a step-through player built in** | **Chosen.** Before/After screenshots cut from the trace: 4 MB instead of 75 MB |

## What we decided
- **Test format:** Sid's kit JSON. Every case is `proposed`, `approved` or `rejected`, and rejected cases keep their reason and stay listed.
- **Only a person decides:** `decide` refuses decisions signed by a model or agent. Several of Sid's kits have approvals by "Claude, for sid".
- **Hosting:** option A on Vercel Pro. The data goes to the public Blob store, walkthrough only (no full trace), with credentials and home-folder paths scrubbed.
- **Tests never go in the `discourse-graph` codebase.**

## What exists now
- **Code:** `~/Desktop/code/proof-kit`, branch `obsidian-runner` off Sid's `proof-runner`. **Nothing is committed yet.** Everything type-checks and 70/70 tests pass. It contains:
  - the Obsidian runner (`--trace`)
  - `propose` (prompt, merge, decide)
  - `publish` (merges into the manifest, scrubs credentials, cuts the walkthrough)
  - `site/index.html` (the catalog page)
- **Proven:** Sid's ENG-2176 kit ran 5/6 with 1 left out because it needs the database. The ENG-2228 kit ran 8/8.
- **Live:** the ENG-2228 walkthrough data is at `discoursegraphs.com/releases/proof/`.
- **Blocker found:** Blob won't serve the catalog page. HTML downloads instead of opening, and scripts are blocked. The page works from any other host, reading the Blob data.

## Next steps
1. **You decide where the page lives:**
   - **`discoursegraphs.com/proof`** (recommended): one static file in the website through a PR. It's only the viewer page, not tests.
   - a separate Vercel project
   - GitHub Pages
2. **You decide on cleanup:** delete the dead `releases/proof/index.html` and `viewer/` files on Blob.
3. **Commit** `obsidian-runner` locally. I've been asking; nothing is committed yet.
4. **Talk to Sid:**
   - share `qa.ts` and its prompt
   - agree where this code lives, given that his PR is still open and the `roam-prototypes` repo is for Roam extensions only
   - a fix for his ENG-2176 kit: its selector matches the tab header before the view
5. **Not proven yet:**
   - a recorded human click on the caption bar actually reaching the runner
   - a negative control: ENG-2228's kit should fail on the build from before the change
   - database setup steps in Obsidian
6. **The research write-up for the ticket:** the comparison, the format and this demo. It could also go to Michael as a hand-off document.

Do you want to start with where the page lives?

# Checkpoint — record session context

Persist the **reasoning layer** of this work session (goal, decisions, dead ends,
constraints, next step) to the Obsidian vault, keyed to the current worktree.
Files are plain markdown written directly — no MCP, no Obsidian required running.

## Steps

### 1. Resolve where to write
Run the helper from the current worktree:

```bash
bash ~/.claude/scripts/session-context.sh resolve
```

It prints `TICKET`, `BRANCH`, `WORKTREE`, `SESSION_DIR`, `CONTEXT_FILE`,
`LOG_FILE`, `STAMP`, `CONTEXT_EXISTS` and creates the folders. **Only write to the
`CONTEXT_FILE` and `LOG_FILE` paths it gives you** — never elsewhere in the vault.
If it errors (not a git repo / detached HEAD), tell the user and stop.

### 2. Read existing context if present
If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=yes`, read `CONTEXT_FILE` first so you UPDATE it rather than
overwrite history. Digest sections get rewritten; accreting sections get appended.

### 3. Gather the reasoning layer
Reconstruct from this session's conversation + git. If a ticket id is present and
Linear is available, you may fetch the title/URL with `mcp__linear-server__get_issue`.
Apply the **extraction rubric** below to decide what is worth recording.

### 4. Write `_context.md`
Use the template at `~/.claude/skills/checkpoint/template.md` as the structure.
- If new file: fill the template. Set `created`/`updated` to today, `sessions: 1`.
- If updating: rewrite digest sections (TL;DR, Approved plan, Current state, Next
  step, Open questions, key_files, status), **append** to accreting sections (Key
  decisions, Dead ends, Constraints, Gotchas, Interventions) with a dated bullet,
  bump `updated` to today and increment `sessions`.
- **Approved plan:** write it only when the user approves a plan (gate 1), verbatim
  as approved: Mermaid diagram, per-file/module intent bullets, and the exact line
  `ship_when_verified: yes|no` (`no` unless the user said ship when verified).
  /create-pr parses this heading and line; don't rename or reformat them.
- **Interventions:** append `- [YYYY-MM-DD] <what the human had to do> — <why the agent couldn't>`
  whenever the user had to step in.

### 5. Append a log snapshot
Write a short dated entry to `LOG_FILE` (a fresh file — no append needed):
a 3–6 line summary of what THIS session accomplished + what changed since last time.
This is the immutable audit trail; `_context.md` is the living digest.

### 6. Confirm
Tell the user what you wrote (context file + log file paths) and the one-line Next step.

## Extraction rubric — what to record (keep it concise)

**The test:** record a line only if it would otherwise have to be *re-derived* or
would prevent *repeating a mistake*. Ask: *"What do I know now that I didn't at
session start, that isn't already in Linear, git, or the code?"*

**DO record (the reasoning layer — it evaporates when the session ends):**
- Scope agreement: how the ticket was interpreted, what's in/out of scope.
- Decisions: what + why + what was rejected + what would make us revisit it.
- Dead ends: what was tried that failed, and why.
- Constraints/preferences the user stated ("ship by Fri", "don't touch billing").
- Gotchas: environmental facts learned the hard way.
- Next step + open questions + current status.

**Do NOT record (noise / lives elsewhere):**
- Activity logs ("edited foo.ts, ran tests") — record outcomes, not keystrokes.
- Anything copy-pasteable from the diff, git history, or the Linear ticket body.
- Resolved questions — delete them or fold the answer into a decision.
- Restating how the code works — that's what the code is for.

**Mark uncertainty** explicitly (`*assumed*`, `*unchecked*`). Prefer 8 sharp lines
over 40 vague ones — this must stay skimmable for the user, not just parseable by an agent.

content.text:
Yes, and it fits the regression goal better than per-PR kits. The idea is **one living suite organised by feature**. PRs then propose *changes* to that suite instead of creating new kits.

## The shape

```
suite/
  obsidian/
    canvas-links.json        ← feature: cases + the code paths that feature lives in
    node-format.json
    node-search.json
  roam/
    discourse-context.json
    …
```

**Each feature file:** Sid's kit format with two additions:
- `files`: globs for the code the feature lives in, e.g. `apps/obsidian/src/components/canvas/**`. This is the feature-map idea from Cursor's skill, plus the code index Cursor's version lacks.
- **History on every case:** which ticket or PR added it and which last changed it, alongside the existing decision record.

**Example:** ENG-2228's 9 cases become part of `obsidian/canvas-links`, and ENG-2176's become part of `obsidian/node-format`. Per-ticket kits stop being the thing we keep.

## What that unlocks

| Need | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Full suite** | Run every approved case in the app, nightly or on each merge to `main`. The catalog shows each feature's health on `main` |
| **PR regression subset** | Match the diff's files against each feature's `files` and run those features' cases. `propose` covers anything new the globs don't catch |
| **Knowing which tests to update** | When a PR touches a feature's files, its cases are marked *needs review*. When a case fails on a PR, the reviewer chooses: regression (fix the code) or intended change (update the case, with the reason recorded) |
| **Coverage gaps** | A feature with no cases, or code no feature's `files` match, shows up as uncovered |

**The PR flow becomes:**
1. `propose` writes a **change set** against the suite: new cases, edited cases, retired cases.
2. You approve or reject each change.
3. The PR runs its affected features plus the change set.
4. When the PR merges, `promote` folds the approved change set into the suite.

## Where the suite lives

| | Separate git repo (e.g. `DiscourseGraphs/proof-suite`) | Vercel Blob |
|---|---|---|
| Out of the `discourse-graph` codebase | ✅ | ✅ |
| History and blame ("who changed this case, and why") | ✅ | ❌ unless we build versioning |
| Reviewing test changes like code | ✅ PRs on the suite | ❌ |
| Size | Small JSON, fits git easily | — |
| Run artifacts (frames, results) | ❌ keep these on Blob | ✅ |

**Recommendation:** suite definitions in a small separate repo, run artifacts on Blob as now. That reverses my earlier "start with Blob only", because a long-lived suite needs history and review.

## Costs to know about
- **Cases interfere with each other in a long run.** Notes, canvases and settings leak from one case into the next. Each feature needs its own setup and cleanup. Fresh vaults per run would be safest; my ENG-2228 kit already creates its own canvas.
- **Run time:** about 1 minute per 8 cases in Obsidian. A few hundred cases means the full suite runs nightly, while PRs run only the affected features.
- **Roam** needs a signed-in test graph for a full run, so local runs only until CI exists.

## What to build
1. Suite layout and a migration of the two existing kits into it.
2. `select --diff` to pick the affected features.
3. A runner mode that runs a set of features, not just one kit.
4. `propose` writing change sets, and `promote`.
5. The catalog grouped by app and feature, showing "`main`" and "this PR" side by side.

**Decision needed:** suite definitions in a separate repo, or Blob only? If a repo, which name, and is creating it in the DiscourseGraphs org OK? That's an action outside this machine, so I'd need your go-ahead. The catalog-hosting question from before is still open too.

import subprocess, fnmatch, re
features = {
  "obsidian/canvas-links": ["apps/obsidian/src/components/canvas/**", "patches/tldraw*", "patches/@tldraw*"],
  "obsidian/node-format": ["apps/obsidian/src/utils/createNode.ts", "apps/obsidian/src/components/DiscourseContextView.tsx", "packages/database/src/lib/*ormat*", "packages/database/src/lib/extractContentFromTitle*"],

}
skip = re.compile(r"(__tests__|\.test\.|\.md$|pnpm-lock|package\.json$|CHANGELOG)")
log = subprocess.run(["git","log","origin/main","--first-parent","-n","25","--format=%h\t%s","--","apps/obsidian"],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.strip().split("\n")
uncovered_total = {}
for line in log:

    unc = [f for f in files if not any(fnmatch.fnmatch(f,g) for gs in features.values() for g in gs)]
    for f in unc: d="/".join(f.split("/")[:4]); uncovered_total[d]=uncovered_total.get(d,0)+1
    print(f"{subject[:58]:58} | {', '.join(sorted(n.split('/')[1] for n in hit)) or '—':28} | uncovered {len(unc)}/{len(files)}")
print("\nmost-changed code no feature covers:")
for d,n in sorted(uncovered_total.items(), key=lambda x:-x[1])[:8]: print(f"  {n:3}  {d}")
EOF

content.text: <total_tokens>14988191 tokens left</total_tokens>

Yes, both are possible. Selecting a PR's cases from the diff works if each feature is defined by the files where users meet it (its UI entry points), not by a folder. And maintaining the suite on Blob works if we rebuild the few things git would have given us. Both tests were ad-hoc scripts over real PR history; nothing is built yet.

## 1. Selecting cases from the diff: what the replay showed

**Matching by folder fails in both directions.**
- The most-changed Obsidian code is shared logic in `src/utils` (32 of the changes across those 25 PRs: sync, import, relations, formats). No UI folder pattern covers it, so those PRs selected nothing.
- `canvas/**` picked the links feature for every canvas PR, including ones that only changed the relation menu.

**Following imports works,** once two adjustments are made:
- Start from the changed files and walk up to the UI entry points that import them.
- Ignore `import type` lines, which don't run code.
- Stop at hub files like the plugin's main class (`src/index.ts`). Without that stop, every change reached every feature.

Results on real PRs:
- **UI-only PRs selected one feature:** ENG-2266 → advanced node search; ENG-2228 and ENG-2256 → canvas.
- **Shared-logic PRs selected 3–4 features:** ENG-2176 picked search, canvas, import and node creation. Sid's generator listed those same areas as at risk for that PR.

**Proposed approach:**
- The import graph supplies the candidate features. It's deterministic and fast.
- `propose` then prunes or adds cases within those features, giving a reason for each.
- The run plan shows why each case was picked, e.g. "selected because `extractContentFromTitle.ts` changed, which `DiscourseContextView` imports".

## 2. Keeping the suite on Blob
Blob has no history, no review step and no safe concurrent editing, so the suite would rebuild a small subset of git:

```
releases/proof/suite/
  refs/main.json            ← the only file that changes: feature → current version. Swapped with
                               a conditional write (ifMatch), so two people can't overwrite each other
  objects/<sha256>.json     ← each version of a feature file; never changes once written
  log/<n>-<time>.json       ← one entry per change: which cases changed, before/after, who, why,
                               PR and ticket, monorepo commit. Gives history, blame and revert
  changesets/pr-<n>.json    ← a PR's proposed new/edited/retired cases, each tied to the version it edits
```

**Lifecycle:**
1. `propose` writes the PR's change set.
2. You decide on each case.
3. The PR runs the affected features from `main` plus its change set.
4. On merge, `promote` folds the change set into `main`. If someone else changed the same feature meanwhile, the version check flags a conflict to re-decide instead of overwriting.
5. Revert means pointing `refs/main` back at an older version.

**Staying in step with the monorepo,** which was your concern with the separate repo:
- **Fewer things can drift:** features are pinned to a few entry files, not folder patterns.
- **A nightly `suite doctor` on `main`** flags:
  - entry files that moved, proposing the new path from git's rename detection
  - changed code that reaches no feature (uncovered)
  - cases failing on `main` because a selector broke rather than the product. Sid's report already tells "the kit needs fixing" apart from "the product failed".
- **Every run records** both the suite version and the monorepo commit, so a result always says which tests ran against which code.

**What we give up compared with a repo:**
- Reviewing test changes happens in the catalog (change-set diffs) and the `decide` command, not in GitHub PR review.
- Only people or CI holding the Blob token can write.
- The versioning layer is ours to maintain, though it's small: one ref file, content-addressed objects, a log.

## Suggested build order
1. Suite layout plus importing the two existing kits as the first features.
2. `suite select --diff` (import graph, hub cutoff, reasons), replayed against these 25 PRs as a check.
3. Change sets and `promote`, with the conflict check.
4. Runner mode for a set of features.
5. Catalog grouped by feature, with history.
6. Nightly `doctor`.

content.text:
Those four folders work like a tiny git, with one shared snapshot of the whole suite. A walk-through with one PR shows it best.

## The pieces
- **`objects/`** holds snapshots of one feature's cases, each named by a hash of its contents. They never change. Editing a feature means writing a *new* snapshot next to the old one.
- **`refs/main.json`** is a table of contents: for each feature, which snapshot is current on `main`. It's the only file that's ever overwritten.

```json
// refs/main.json, suite version 41
{ "version": 41,
  "features": {
    "obsidian/canvas":      "objects/a1b2….json",
    "obsidian/node-format": "objects/c3d4….json" } }
```

"Updating the suite" therefore always means: write the new snapshot, then rewrite this small table to point at it.

**What "swapped with a conditional write" means:**
- The table is rewritten with a check that says "only if it's still version 41".
- If someone else changed it first (say to 42), the write is refused instead of silently wiping their change.

## A PR from start to finish
Say ENG-2500 (PR #1600) changes how canvas links behave.

**1. Proposing.** `propose` writes `changesets/pr-1600.json`. It never touches `main`.
```json
{ "pr": 1600, "ticket": "ENG-2500", "base": { "obsidian/canvas": "objects/a1b2….json" },
  "add":    [ { "case": { "id": "dw1-link-opens-in-new-tab", … }, "decision": "proposed" } ],
  "edit":   [ { "id": "text-open-link", "change": "expect a new tab, not the same one",
                "kind": "behaviour", "decision": "proposed" } ],
  "retire": [] }
```

**2. Deciding.** You approve or reject each entry. Nothing on `main` changes.

**3. Running the PR.** The runner takes the affected features from `main` and applies the change set on top in memory, then runs against the PR's build. Results go under `runs/pr-1600/…`. The catalog shows "`main`" next to "this PR".

**4. Merging:** `promote` runs.
1. Build the new canvas snapshot: the old one plus the approved additions and edits.
2. Write it as `objects/e5f6….json`.
3. Rewrite `refs/main.json` so canvas points at `e5f6…`, conditional on it still being version 41. It becomes version 42.
4. Write `log/42-….json`: which cases were added or edited, before and after, who approved them, and the PR and commit.

**5. If the PR is closed without merging,** its change set is simply abandoned. `main` never saw it.

So the answers to your questions:
- **New tests for a PR:** they sit in that PR's change set until the PR merges, then join the feature's snapshot on `main`.
- **Updates to old tests:** they go into the same change set as edits tied to the snapshot they started from. The old version stays in its old snapshot forever. The log records why it changed, so you can see a case's history or revert it.

## What to do about regressions
When a PR run fails a case the PR didn't change, someone has to classify it before merge. There are three outcomes:

| What it is | What happens | Effect on the suite |
|---|---|---|
| **Real regression:** the PR broke something | Fix the code and rerun | None; the case stays as it is |
| **Intended change:** the old expectation is now wrong | Add an edit to the change set with `kind: "behaviour"` and a reason; a person approves it | Updated on merge; the log shows the expectation changed on purpose |
| **Broken test:** behaviour is the same but a selector or step broke | Add an edit with `kind: "test-fix"` | Updated on merge, labelled as maintenance, not a behaviour change |

Sid's report can already tell "the kit needs fixing" apart from "the product failed", which helps a person classify.

**Catching what PR selection misses:**
- The **nightly full-suite run on `main`** catches regressions whose PR didn't select the affected case.
- When a case flips from pass to fail on `main`, every run records its monorepo commit. So the catalog can list the PRs merged between the last passing run and the first failing one, and those are the suspects.

**Two PRs editing the same case:**
- Whichever merges first wins.
- The second one's `promote` sees that its starting snapshot is no longer current. It stops and asks for that edit to be redone against the new version, rather than overwriting the first PR's change.

content.text:
Fair point. I used `main` for two different things, and only one of them involves the monorepo.

**1. `refs/main.json` is just a name for the suite's current approved version.** It's a file on Blob and has nothing to do with git. Calling it `refs/current.json` or `approved.json` would be clearer, and I'll rename it.

**2. The monorepo's `main` branch is something the suite reads from but never writes to.** The Blob suite touches the monorepo in exactly three read-only ways:
- **To pick cases:** reading a PR's diff (`git diff`) to find the affected features.
- **To run cases:** building the plugin from a branch, either the PR's branch or the monorepo's `main` for the nightly run, and testing it.
- **To label results:** recording which monorepo commit each run tested.

Nothing is ever written into the monorepo. No files, commits or branches.

**Why the two are still linked:** the suite's approved version should describe how the app behaves *on the monorepo's `main` branch*.
- When a PR is still open, its new or edited cases stay in its change set, because that behaviour isn't on `main` yet.
- When the PR **merges into the monorepo's main**, that's the signal to `promote` its change set into the suite's approved version.
- If the PR is closed unmerged, the suite never changes.

The merge is only a trigger. Someone runs `promote` after merging, or CI does it later. The suite itself stays entirely on Blob.

Renamed, the layout reads:
```
suite/
  approved.json          ← which version of each feature is current (tracks what's merged)
  objects/…              ← every version of every feature, never changed
  log/…                  ← history of changes
  changesets/pr-1600…    ← a PR's proposed cases, waiting for that PR to merge
```

# Hand-off document

Produces one published HTML Artifact that someone else can read without you in the room.

## Before writing

1. Invoke `dg-engineering-writing-style` as a Skill. It owns the prose rules; this skill owns the
   structure. Do not restate or copy its guidance here — it is read at runtime so it cannot drift.
2. Invoke `artifact-design` as a Skill before writing the file.
3. Author `.html`, never `.md`. Markdown cannot do collapsible sections, which this format needs.

## Structure — high level first

Michael reads top-down and stops when he has enough. The page must answer the question before it
justifies the answer.

1. **Masthead** — ticket id, one-line subject, date, and what state the work is in
   (e.g. "research only, no code changed").
2. **Verdict block, above the fold.** The recommendation as a heading in plain words, then two
   short paragraphs: why, and what the losing option's one real merit is and how to buy it more
   cheaply. Never open with background or methodology.
3. **Table of contents**, as a sticky rail on wide screens. Numbered sections.
4. **Collapsible sections** (`<details>`/`<summary>`), one per numbered item, each with a one-line
   subtitle under its heading saying what is inside. Open the first; collapse the rest. Provide
   Expand all / Collapse all. A TOC click opens its target section.
5. **Comparison tables** rather than prose, whenever two or more options are weighed. One row per
   dimension, one column per option, a short verdict pill in each cell before the explanation.

## Be concise

Length is a cost the reader pays. Lead with the point; expand only where the point is not
self-evident.

- **Bullets before prose.** A section opens with the main points as bullets, one idea each, bolded
  lead clause first. Prose comes after, and only to say something the bullets could not.
- **Simple sentences.** One clause carrying one fact. Split anything joined by "and" or a
  semicolon that is really two statements.
- **Three paragraphs is the ceiling** for any section, unless the reader asked for depth. If a
  section needs more, it is really two sections, or the extra belongs in a source toggle.
- **Push detail down, not out.** Supporting evidence, line numbers and reasoning go in a source
  toggle (below) or a sub-paragraph under the bullet it supports. Nothing is deleted for brevity;
  it is moved somewhere skippable.
- **Answer the question asked, in its own words.** When the reader asks two questions, the section
  gets two headings that repeat their questions back. Do not reorganise their question into your
  own framing.

## Provenance — always, but ignorable

Every claim that rests on a measurement, a file, a command, or a test carries its source. Michael
cares about provenance; he does not want to read it on the way past.

Put each one in an inline `<details class="prov"><summary>source</summary>` toggle immediately
after the claim, rendered small, monospace and muted. Say once, under the verdict, that the
toggles exist and the brief reads straight through without them.

What goes in a source toggle:

- **File and line**, as read, not as remembered — `StoreSchema.ts:202`, `uiOverrides.tsx:738`.
- **The command**, where a number came from a count or a grep. Quote it so it can be re-run.
- **How a version or date was established** — distinguish what you verified yourself from what you
  took from release notes or a subagent. Label the weaker one as such, visibly.
- **What a test actually did**, including the failures on the way, when they tell the reader
  something about the shape of the problem.
- **Judgement, labelled as judgement.** Where a severity or an estimate is inferred rather than
  measured, say so in the toggle. This is the most valuable kind, because it is the kind the reader
  would otherwise have to guess at.
- **Corrections.** Where an earlier figure or claim was wrong, state the old one, the new one, and
  why the new one is better. Do not silently replace it.

Never pad a toggle. If a claim has no source beyond reasoning, write the reasoning in one line.

## Open items

Give unresolved things their own named place near the end — not a caveat buried mid-paragraph. For
each: what is not known, why it could not be settled, and what it costs if the guess is wrong.
A claim you could not verify is stated as unverified in the body too, not only in the appendix.

## After publishing

Tell the user the artifact is private and must be shared from the page's Share menu before anyone
else can open it.

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.
